title: Max Increase to Keep City Skyline
statement:
A city is an `n x n` grid of blocks with one building per block; `grid[r][c]` is the height of the building in row `r`, column `c`. Looking at the city from the north or south, you see the tallest building of every column; looking from the east or west, you see the tallest building of every row. These outlines are the skylines.

You may raise any buildings (including ones of height 0) by any non-negative amounts, each chosen independently, as long as all four skylines look exactly the same afterwards. Return the largest possible sum of all the raises.
notes:
## Intuition

Raising buildings one unit at a time and re-checking the skylines works, but it is slow. The skyline from north or south is the tallest building of each column, and from east or west the tallest of each row. A building at `(r, c)` can grow until it would become taller than the tallest in its row or in its column, so its best height is the smaller of those two maxima. Raising it that far never changes any maximum, and every building can be raised independently, so taking each building to its own limit gives the largest total.

## Approach

1. Scan the grid once, recording each row's maximum in `rowMax` and each column's maximum in `colMax`.
2. Scan again. For each cell, `limit = min(rowMax[r], colMax[c])`.
3. Add `limit - grid[r][c]` to `total` (never negative, because the cell is part of both maxima).
4. Return `total`.

## Example 1, step by step

For `[[3,0,8,4],[2,4,5,7],[9,2,6,3],[0,3,1,0]]`, `rowMax = [8,7,9,3]` and `colMax = [9,4,8,7]`. Row 0 gets limits `8,4,8,7`, adding `5+4+0+3 = 12`; row 1 gets `7,4,7,7`, adding `5+0+2+0 = 7`; row 2 gets `9,4,8,7`, adding `0+2+2+4 = 8`; row 3 gets `3,3,3,3`, adding `3+0+2+3 = 8`. The `total` is `12 + 7 + 8 + 8 = 35`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n²): two passes over the `n x n` grid.
- Space: O(n): one maximum per row and per column.

## Pitfalls

- Use the minimum of the two maxima, not the maximum: exceeding either one changes a skyline.
- Compute all maxima before raising anything; updating the grid while scanning would mix old and new heights.
- The four directions need only two arrays, because north and south (and east and west) show the same maxima.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | side length of the grid |
| `rowMax` | tallest building in each row (east and west skylines) |
| `colMax` | tallest building in each column (north and south skylines) |
| `r`, `c` | current row and column |
| `limit` | highest the building at `(r, c)` may become |
| `total` | sum of all raises so far |

narration.2: The grid is square, so n is both the number of rows and of columns.
narration.3: rowMax[r] will hold the tallest building in row r, which is what the east and west skylines show.
narration.4: colMax[c] will hold the tallest building in column c, which is what the north and south skylines show.
narration.7: Update the maximum of this row with the current building.
narration.8: Update the maximum of this column with the current building.
narration.11: total accumulates how much the buildings can be raised altogether.
narration.14: The building may grow up to the smaller of its row and column maxima without changing either skyline.
narration.15: Raise it all the way to that limit and add the increase to the total.
narration.18: Every building is at its own highest allowed height, so this sum is the maximum.
